name: AWS
tagline: Private VPC, TLS load balancers, SSM access and CloudFront: a web stack.

howItWorks.title: What it is and where it sits
howItWorks.body:
AWS is on-demand infrastructure: networks, compute, load balancers and managed services behind one API.
VPC routing is L3, NLB balances at L4, ALB terminates TLS and routes at L7.
A Region holds several Availability Zones; spread every tier across at least two.
Everything is an API call, so the CLI, Terraform and the console build the same objects.
Shared responsibility: AWS runs the hardware, you configure access, patching and data.

howItWorks.title: Network components (VPC)
howItWorks.body:
A VPC is a private CIDR; subnets live in one AZ each.
Public subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway; private subnets route to a NAT gateway.
Security groups are stateful and attach to interfaces; network ACLs are stateless per subnet.
VPC endpoints reach S3, SSM and others privately without NAT.
Route 53 resolves names; alias records point at ALB, NLB and CloudFront.

howItWorks.title: Request flow
howItWorks.body:
Route 53 resolves the domain to CloudFront or a load balancer.
The load balancer in a public subnet accepts the connection and terminates TLS with ACM.
It forwards to a healthy target in a private subnet; the app security group admits only the LB group.
Targets reach the internet outbound through NAT, never inbound.
Logs and metrics flow to CloudWatch; alarms notify through SNS.

howItWorks.title: Configuration and identity model
howItWorks.body:
IAM roles give instances and pods temporary credentials; avoid long-lived access keys.
Policies are JSON: principal, action, resource, condition. Explicit deny wins.
Tags drive cost allocation and automation; name and tag from day one.
SSM Parameter Store and Secrets Manager hold secrets; user-data and images never do.
Describe the stack as code (CLI scripts, CloudFormation or Terraform) so it is repeatable.

howItWorks.title: Connecting to its neighbours
howItWorks.body:
In front: Route 53 aliases, CloudFront and the public load balancer receive users.
Behind: target groups point at EC2 instances, container IPs or Lambda functions.
ALB works at L7 with host and path rules and ACM certificates; NLB forwards TCP, UDP or TLS at L4.
On Kubernetes, instance targets hit a NodePort on each worker; IP targets hit pod IPs directly.
Security groups chain: the app group admits only the load balancer group.

howItWorks.title: High availability and scaling
howItWorks.body:
Spread subnets and targets across two or three AZs; one NAT gateway per AZ avoids a single choke point.
Auto Scaling groups replace failed instances and scale on metrics; use launch templates.
Multi-AZ managed databases fail over automatically; back up with snapshots.
CloudFront caches static content at the edge and absorbs spikes.
Use health checks at both LB and Auto Scaling levels.

howItWorks.title: Security
howItWorks.body:
Least-privilege IAM, MFA on humans, no root user for daily work.
Private subnets for servers; only load balancers and NAT sit in public subnets.
SSM Session Manager replaces SSH: no key, no open port 22, every session auditable.
Enforce IMDSv2, S3 Block Public Access and encryption at rest with KMS.
CloudTrail records API calls; GuardDuty and Config flag risky behaviour.

howItWorks.title: Observability
howItWorks.body:
CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms; EC2 memory and disk need the CloudWatch agent.
Alarm on UnHealthyHostCount, ALB 5XX and TargetResponseTime, notify with SNS.
Enable ALB access logs to S3 and VPC Flow Logs for network questions.
CloudTrail answers who changed what; Cost Explorer and budgets catch surprise bills.

howItWorks.title: Failure modes and troubleshooting
howItWorks.body:
Unhealthy targets: app security group lacks the LB group, wrong health-check path or port.
502 from ALB means the target closed the connection; 504 means it timed out.
No outbound from private subnets: check the route to NAT and the NAT's subnet route to IGW.
SSM session will not start: instance role missing or no path to the SSM endpoints.
Use Reachability Analyzer to trace a path between two resources.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
Load balancing: NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik or Caddy on EC2 when you need custom routing.
Compute and network: Azure, Google Cloud, or on-premises KVM, ESXi and OpenStack.
Identity and secrets: Keycloak or Okta; Vault or SOPS beside Secrets Manager.
Metrics: Prometheus and Grafana or Datadog instead of CloudWatch.
Infrastructure as code: Terraform, OpenTofu, CloudFormation or Pulumi.

flow: Browser resolves the domain in Route 53.
Static paths hit CloudFront, which fetches from private S3 through OAC.
App paths reach the ALB in a public subnet over HTTPS.
ALB terminates TLS with ACM and forwards HTTP to a healthy target.
Nginx in Docker proxies to the app container on a private bridge.
The app reads Parameter Store and reaches external services through NAT.
CloudWatch evaluates metrics and SNS notifies on alarm.

deploy.summary: Build the stack with AWS CLI v2 in one shell. NAT and ALB bill hourly; run the cleanup.
prerequisites: AWS CLI v2 configured with a non-root identity
Route 53 hosted zone for your domain (placeholders: ZONE_ID, DOMAIN)

steps.title: 1. VPC, subnets, IGW, NAT and routes
steps.code:
export AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 AWS_PAGER=""
AZ_A=${AWS_REGION}a; AZ_B=${AWS_REGION}b
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/16 --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=demo-vpc}]' --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --vpc-id $VPC --enable-dns-hostnames
PUB_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/24  --availability-zone $AZ_A --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
PUB_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.20.1.0/24  --availability-zone $AZ_B --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
PRIV_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.20.10.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ_A --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
PRIV_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.20.11.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ_B --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id $IGW --vpc-id $VPC
PUB_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PUB_RT --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PUB_RT --subnet-id $PUB_A
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PUB_RT --subnet-id $PUB_B
EIP=$(aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc --query AllocationId --output text)
NAT=$(aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id $PUB_A --allocation-id $EIP --query NatGateway.NatGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 wait nat-gateway-available --nat-gateway-ids $NAT
NAT_IP=$(aws ec2 describe-addresses --allocation-ids $EIP --query 'Addresses[0].PublicIp' --output text)
PRIV_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PRIV_RT --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id $NAT
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PRIV_RT --subnet-id $PRIV_A
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PRIV_RT --subnet-id $PRIV_B
echo "Allow-list in MongoDB database: $NAT_IP/32"
steps.note: Add $NAT_IP/32 to the database IP access list. In production run one NAT per AZ.

steps.title: 2. Security groups and instance role
steps.code:
ALB_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name demo-alb-sg --description ALB --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text)
APP_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name demo-app-sg --description App --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $ALB_SG --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $APP_SG --protocol tcp --port 80 --source-group $ALB_SG
cat > trust.json <<'EOF'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}
EOF
cat > params.json <<'EOF'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["ssm:GetParameter"],"Resource":"arn:aws:ssm:*:*:parameter/demo/*"}]}
EOF
aws iam create-role --role-name demo-ssm-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name demo-ssm-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name demo-ssm-role --policy-name demo-params --policy-document file://params.json
aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name demo-ssm-profile
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name demo-ssm-profile --role-name demo-ssm-role
sleep 15
steps.note: No rule opens port 22. A customer-managed KMS key also needs kms:Decrypt on the role.

steps.title: 3. Store the secret in Parameter Store
steps.note: Replace the placeholder with your own connection string. The default aws/ssm KMS key encrypts it.

steps.title: 4. Private EC2 with Docker Compose and Nginx
steps.code:
AMI=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 --query Parameter.Value --output text)
cat > userdata.sh <<'UD'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y docker
systemctl enable --now docker
mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins /opt/app
curl -SL https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.29.7/docker-compose-linux-x86_64 -o /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose
chmod +x /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose
cat > /opt/app/nginx.conf <<'NG'
server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://app:5678; proxy_set_header Host $host; } }
NG
cat > /opt/app/compose.yaml <<'CY'
services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    volumes: ["./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro"]
    networks: [front, back]
    restart: always
  app:
    image: hashicorp/http-echo:1.0
    command: ["-text=hello from app"]
    networks: [back]
    restart: always
networks:
  front: {driver: bridge}
  back: {driver: bridge}
CY
cd /opt/app && docker compose up -d
UD
I1=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id $AMI --instance-type t3.micro --subnet-id $PRIV_A --security-group-ids $APP_SG \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=demo-ssm-profile --metadata-options HttpTokens=required,HttpPutResponseHopLimit=2 --user-data file://userdata.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=demo-app-a}]' --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids $I1
steps.note: Nginx joins both bridge networks; the app joins only back. A real app reads DB_URL with aws ssm get-parameter --with-decryption.

steps.title: 5. ACM certificate, HTTPS ALB and Route 53 alias
steps.code:
DOMAIN=app.example.com; ZONE_ID=ZXXXXXXXXXXXX   # placeholders
CERT=$(aws acm request-certificate --domain-name $DOMAIN --validation-method DNS --query CertificateArn --output text)
sleep 15
read CN CV < <(aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn $CERT --query 'Certificate.DomainValidationOptions[0].ResourceRecord.[Name,Value]' --output text)
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id $ZONE_ID --change-batch "{\"Changes\":[{\"Action\":\"UPSERT\",\"ResourceRecordSet\":{\"Name\":\"$CN\",\"Type\":\"CNAME\",\"TTL\":300,\"ResourceRecords\":[{\"Value\":\"$CV\"}]}}]}"
aws acm wait certificate-validated --certificate-arn $CERT
TG=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --name demo-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC --target-type instance --health-check-path / --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 register-targets --target-group-arn $TG --targets Id=$I1
ALB=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name demo-alb --subnets $PUB_A $PUB_B --security-groups $ALB_SG --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn $ALB --protocol HTTPS --port 443 --certificates CertificateArn=$CERT --ssl-policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG
aws elbv2 wait load-balancer-available --load-balancer-arns $ALB
read ALB_DNS ALB_ZONE < <(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --load-balancer-arns $ALB --query 'LoadBalancers[0].[DNSName,CanonicalHostedZoneId]' --output text)
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id $ZONE_ID --change-batch "{\"Changes\":[{\"Action\":\"UPSERT\",\"ResourceRecordSet\":{\"Name\":\"$DOMAIN\",\"Type\":\"A\",\"AliasTarget\":{\"HostedZoneId\":\"$ALB_ZONE\",\"DNSName\":\"$ALB_DNS\",\"EvaluateTargetHealth\":true}}}]}"
steps.note: The domain must live in your Route 53 zone. Validation usually completes within minutes.

steps.title: 6. Reach the instance with SSM
steps.code:
aws ssm describe-instance-information --query 'InstanceInformationList[].InstanceId'
aws ssm start-session --target $I1
steps.note: The instance appears within minutes. Inside the shell run docker ps to see both containers.

steps.title: 7. Private S3 behind CloudFront with OAC
steps.code:
BUCKET=demo-static-$(uuidgen | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | cut -c1-12) aws s3api create-bucket --bucket $BUCKET --region $AWS_REGION --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=$AWS_REGION echo '

React build goes here

' > index.html aws s3 cp index.html s3://$BUCKET/index.html --content-type text/html OAC=$(aws cloudfront create-origin-access-control --origin-access-control-config "Name=demo-oac-$BUCKET,SigningProtocol=sigv4,SigningBehavior=always,OriginAccessControlOriginType=s3" --query OriginAccessControl.Id --output text) cat > cf.json < bucket-policy.json <
steps.note: Needs bash. 658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6 is the managed CachingOptimized policy.

steps.title: 8. CloudWatch alarm through SNS
steps.code:
TOPIC=$(aws sns create-topic --name demo-alerts --query TopicArn --output text)
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $TOPIC --protocol email --notification-endpoint you@example.com   # placeholder
TG_DIM=${TG##*:}; ALB_DIM=${ALB#*:loadbalancer/}
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name demo-unhealthy-targets --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name UnHealthyHostCount --statistic Maximum \
  --dimensions Name=TargetGroup,Value=$TG_DIM Name=LoadBalancer,Value=$ALB_DIM --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 --threshold 1 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching --alarm-actions $TOPIC
steps.note: Confirm the email subscription first. Test by running docker stop on the nginx container via SSM.

verify: curl -I https://$DOMAIN/ returns 200 with a valid ACM certificate.
curl -I https://$DIST_DOMAIN/ returns 200; the direct S3 URL returns 403.
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names demo-unhealthy-targets shows OK, then ALARM on failure.
pitfalls: NAT gateways and ALBs bill hourly; forgotten ones are the classic surprise bill.
External services that allow-list IPs reject you if they lack the current NAT Elastic IP.
SSM needs an outbound path (NAT or VPC endpoints) and the instance role.
Unhealthy targets usually mean the app security group omits the ALB group.
ACM certificates for an ALB must be in the ALB's region.
CloudFront caches index.html; invalidate it after each frontend deploy.
Health checks on the wrong port or path mark every target unhealthy at once.
keyPoints: Public subnets hold only load balancers and NAT; servers stay private.
ALB routes at L7, NLB at L4; targets are instances or pod IPs.
SSM Session Manager replaces SSH: no key, no open port 22.
CloudWatch alarms notify through SNS; secrets live in Parameter Store.
quickDeploy: Create VPC, subnets, IGW, NAT and route tables.
Launch private EC2 with an SSM role.
Add ACM certificate, HTTPS ALB and Route 53 alias.
Wire CloudFront, CloudWatch and SNS alarms.
osiNote: Routes subnets at L3, balances TCP at L4, terminates TLS at L7.
production: One NAT gateway per AZ; allow-list its Elastic IP at external services.
Spread targets across two AZs; health-check the ALB target group.
Keep secrets in SSM Parameter Store as SecureString; never in user-data.
Enforce IMDSv2, security-group chaining and S3 Block Public Access.
Alarm on UnHealthyHostCount, ALB 5XX and target response time.
